label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article II, Section 3. The President gives Congress information of the state of the Union and recommends measures to it; on extraordinary occasions he may convene both houses or either of them, and if they disagree about the time of adjournment he may adjourn them to such time as he thinks proper; he receives ambassadors and other public ministers, takes care that the laws be faithfully executed, and commissions all the officers of the United States.
This story is about whether the executive may charge a person for damaging government property.
In Helvidius No. I (August 24, 1793) Madison, answering Pacificus, wrote that the executive's natural province is executing laws, so its acts must presuppose existing laws.
He poured ball bearings into the fuel tank and struck the plane with an axe.
Airport crew caught him, and he was filmed standing on top of the plane.
The strongest argument against this is that the duty to execute the laws does not reach a charge for damage outside ordinary reach, and that this stretches power the clause does not grant.
We read this clause to mean the executive must take care that existing laws are carried out.
Charging a person for destruction of government property is ordinary enforcement, not new law.
This keeps enforcement with the branch that carries out the laws.
